content.title: Italy Slams the Door on Distant Ancestry Claims in Major Citizenship Crackdown
content.text: 09 Apr 2025 Italy has dramatically tightened its citizenship laws, cutting off access for millions who previously qualified through distant ancestry. The move, aimed at curbing what officials call a “passport rush” driven by convenience rather than cultural connection, has sparked global debate and left thousands of applications in limbo. Law slams door on ancestral claims Italy, long generous in offering citizenship by descent, has dramatically tightened the rules. As of April 2025, only those with an Italian parent or grandparent can now qualify for citizenship through ancestry. The shift marks a sharp reversal from decades of open eligibility that welcomed millions with more distant Italian roots, including great-grandchildren and beyond. The sudden decree blocked access for up to 80 million people worldwide who previously qualified. It immediately upended the hopes of thousands who had invested years, money, and energy into tracing their lineage. Many of those applications now sit in limbo. Courts, consulates swamped by surge The reform follows years of mounting pressure on Italy’s legal and bureaucratic systems. Municipal offices, courts, and consulates reported being overwhelmed by record volumes of citizenship claims. Cities like San Donà di Piave in northern Italy saw local government workers devoting half their time to handling requests from descendants—mostly in Brazil—who, officials said, never intended to visit, let alone live in the country. Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said that the move came after “years of abuses” by people “who had few ties to the country and only coveted its passport.” At a press conference, he emphasized, “Being an Italian citizen is a serious thing. It’s not a game to get a passport in your pocket to go shopping in Miami.” (Image courtesy of Pixabay) Reining in a loophole turned industry Critics within Italy’s right-wing government called the old system a magnet for opportunists and profiteers. A cottage industry emerged to meet the demand, with companies charging thousands of dollars to dig up records and file paperwork. One even advertised a “Black Friday citizenship special.” However, the appeal of an Italian passport was hard to resist. Italy’s document ranks among the strongest in the world for visa-free travel. South America, where millions of Italians once emigrated, became a hotspot for new applications. In 2024 alone, Italy granted citizenship to 30,000 people in Argentina, up from 20,000 in 2023. Brazil saw a similar jump—from 14,000 to 20,000 From global opportunity to national identity Until now, Italy’s citizenship laws leaned heavily on “jus sanguinis,” or right of blood. Anyone with proof of an ancestor alive after 1861—the year Italy became a nation—could apply. That leniency set Italy apart from many European countries, where stricter documentation or language requirements often apply. Now, the government has drawn a line. Only those with direct links—parents or grandparents born in Italy—can use ancestry to become Italian. (Image courtesy of fabiomax via iStock) Change stirs debate across political divide The law has divided Italy’s political spectrum. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s nationalist administration introduced the change, expecting praise. However, some on the political right felt betrayed. They argued that ancestry-based citizenship helps preserve cultural and ethnic identity. Others said that the old law was outdated and ripe for abuse. “Citizenship cannot be automatic for those who have an ancestor who emigrated centuries ago, without any cultural or linguistic ties to the country,” said Tajani. Valentino Larcinese, a public policy expert at the London School of Economics, agreed. “The idea of applying some limits is reasonable,” he said. He noted the real imbalance lies in how Italy treats children of legal immigrants already living in the country. While foreigners could claim Italian nationality based on distant ancestors, Italian-born children of immigrants must wait until age 18—even if they’ve never known another home. Pending cases still on hold The change does not affect about 60,000 applications already in progress. However, officials suggested that those cases will face greater scrutiny. In October 2024, Italy’s Interior Ministry had already begun rejecting claims based on a new interpretation of ancestral eligibility. If an ancestor renounced Italian citizenship while their child was still a minor, that lineage no longer counted—a detail that blindsided many applicants. Rejection notices surged. Online forums filled with frustration. Applicants shared stories of years wasted, thousands spent, and plans abandoned. Some had even moved to Italy, expecting approval. (Image courtesy of Christina Morillo via Pexels) Shift to centralized and in-person processing To reduce delays and prevent fraud, Italy will now handle all applications through a single federal system. Consulates abroad are out. In-person interviews are in. Every applicant must travel to Italy to complete the process, a move expected to reduce speculative filings. Dual nationals also face new responsibilities. To retain their status, they must stay engaged—renewing passports, paying taxes, and voting. A passport, officials said, cannot be a forgotten trophy. A broader global trend Italy’s decision follows a broader reevaluation of citizenship laws across the world. Nationalist movements and rising immigration have prompted countries to reconsider who belongs—and why. In the United States, former President Donald Trump attempted to end birthright citizenship through an executive order in January. A judge blocked the move as unconstitutional, but the debate rages on. Larcinese believed that Italy’s June referendum could signal a deeper shift. One key issue up for vote: whether to cut the naturalization wait time from ten to five years. If passed, it may ease the path for long-term immigrants already living and working in Italy, giving them a route to the same rights granted to overseas descendants under the old system. (Image courtesy of Alina Rosanova via iStock) An evolving travel landscape for visitors and descendants Italy’s abrupt decision to restrict citizenship by descent now limits eligibility to those with Italian parents or grandparents—excluding millions who once qualified through great-grandparents or more distant ties. For short-term and long-term visitors hoping to leverage Italian lineage to simplify travel across the European Union (EU), this effectively closes a popular loophole. Many applicants, especially from South America and the United States, pursued Italian citizenship not to live in Italy, but to access the visa-free mobility that an EU passport offers. As the European Travel Information and Authorization System (ETIAS) nears its full launch, these changes will further stratify who can move freely through the Schengen Area. Non-EU travelers will need ETIAS approval to visit, and those who once expected to bypass this process via Italian ancestry will now face the same screening and approval layers as any other third-country national. For migrants seeking permanence through ancestry, the road has just become steeper—especially since Italian consulates abroad will no longer process citizenship applications, and travel to Italy will now be required for in-person interviews. A recalibration of who deserves to belong Italy’s crackdown on citizenship through distant bloodlines signals a broader shift in EU immigration discourse: moving away from symbolic gestures of ancestral inclusion and toward more grounded, residence-based policies. The move challenges traditional notions of jus sanguinis (citizenship by blood) and reflects growing discomfort with identity tourism—where passports are sought for convenience rather than connection At a policy level, Italy’s stricter stance may catalyze reevaluation across the EU. Critics argue it’s unjust to grant rights to descendants of long-gone emigrants while withholding citizenship from children born and raised within EU borders to immigrant parents. Upcoming legislative discussions in Italy aim to shorten residency requirements for the children or grandchildren of Italian citizens—potentially from five or ten years to just two or three—indicating a pivot toward favoring integration over lineage. This reorientation also speaks to a deeper EU tension: balancing demographic decline and labor needs with national identity and migration control. In light of the surging demand for second passports and mounting administrative strain, countries may begin prioritizing immigration pathways rooted in residency, cultural integration, and labor market contribution—rather than ancestral claims detached from present-day ties. (Image courtesy of Gotta Be Worth It via Pexels) A new era of identity In redefining what it means to be Italian, Rome is drawing a sharp line between heritage and belonging. The latest citizenship decree—cutting off eligibility beyond grandparents and centralizing application processes—marks a shift from nostalgia-driven policy to one rooted in demographic urgency and national pragmatism. While some applaud the move as a necessary response to administrative overload and misuse, others view it as a betrayal of the very diaspora that once symbolized Italian resilience. What remains clear is this: citizenship, once seen as a birthright through blood, is now a privilege earned through presence and participation. As Italy’s population ages and its global footprint expands, the country must balance pride in its past with the pressures of its future. The Italian passport may still open doors, but from now on, only for those willing to walk through them—not just inherit them.
